guide.title: Bayside, Queens: Bell Boulevard, the Bell Farm and Four Landmarks
guide.intro: Bayside is a neighborhood in northeastern Queens, in Community District 11, with Alley Pond Park along its eastern edge and Little Neck Bay to the northeast. The city's landmarks register carries four individual landmarks here: the Lawrence Graveyard at 216th Street and 42nd Avenue, the John William and Lydia Ann Bell Ahles House on 213th Street, Hawthorne Court Apartments on 43rd Avenue and 216th Street, and the cobblestone house at 35-34 Bell Boulevard. The Landmarks Preservation Commission's report on the Ahles House states that "Very few 19th century houses survive in Bayside." The Bayside Village Business Improvement District covers Bell Boulevard between Northern Boulevard and 35th Avenue. Crocheron Park runs along the Cross Island Parkway between 33rd and 35th Avenues, and the Long Island Rail Road's Port Washington Branch calls at Bayside.

sections.heading: Bell Boulevard and the landmark houses
sections.body:
The Bayside Village Business Improvement District defines its district in its own words as "an eight block strip between Northern Blvd. and 35th Avenue along Bell Blvd.", and says it is "served by Community Board #11" and by the 111th Precinct, whose station house is at 45-06 215th Street.

The cobblestone house at 35-34 Bell Boulevard is a designated New York City landmark; the Landmarks Preservation Commission's designation report opens by placing it "on a commercial street in Bayside, Queens." The other three individual landmarks are houses and a burial ground. The John William and Lydia Ann Bell Ahles House, at 39-24 to 39-26 213th Street, is described in its designation report as "the only remaining example of the substantial Second Empire buildings erected in Bayside during the 1870s and 1880s" and as "one of the oldest surviving in Bayside"; the same report records that "Very few 19th century houses survive in Bayside," that the house was moved in 1924 when Christy Street became 213th Street, and that its designation was opposed by its owner for seven years while the Bayside Historical Society, the Community Board 11 Landmarks Committee and Friends of Oakland Lake & Ravine, Inc. pressed for it.

Hawthorne Court Apartments occupies 215-37 to 215-43 43rd Avenue and 42-22 to 42-38 216th Street. Benjamin Braunstein designed it, its brickwork is laid in monk bond and its roofs are jerkinheads, and it took a Queens Chamber of Commerce award in 1931.

Two more houses stand outside the landmarks register. The Cornell-Appleton House at 214-33 33rd Road is, in the wording of the neighborhood's Wikipedia article, "thought to be one of the oldest in Bayside"; Kevin Walsh, writing for Brownstoner and cited as that article's source, dates its construction to 1852 and calls it "venerable, but not as aged as, say, the Lent-Riker House in Jackson Heights or the Onderdonk House in Ridgewood." The Corbett House at 221-04 Corbett Road was the subject of Barney Nagler's New York Times piece of September 1, 1985, "Gentleman In The House On Corbett Road."

sections.heading: The Bell farm, the Lawrence graveyard and the parks
sections.body:
Abraham Bell acquired land in Bayside in 1824 and worked a farm of 246 acres. The Bell family donated the land for the railroad station, and a 95-acre parcel later went to the Bellcourt tract, one of the Rickert-Finlay Realty Company's developments. The Landmarks Preservation Commission's report on 35-34 Bell Boulevard gives the origin of the "Alley" name: "Initially, access was from Little Neck Bay, by boat, or via a road called the “Alley” that ran along the shore." Alley Pond Park borders Bayside along the neighborhood's eastern edge.

The Lawrence Graveyard, at 216th Street and 42nd Avenue, is entered in the Landmarks Preservation Commission's designation list as "LAWRENCE GRAVEYARD, 216th Street and 42nd Avenue, Bayside, Borough of Queens. Built about 1840." That report counts forty-eight graves, the last of them in 1925, and traces the ground to a 1645 patent; among those it names are Cornelius W. Lawrence and Anne Willets, and it describes a twin marker for two McKim children.

Crocheron Park sits along the Cross Island Parkway between 33rd and 35th Avenues, in ZIP 11361. The Parks Department files it as Q012 in Community Board 11 and gives its size as 45.79 acres; its hexagonal gazebos and the Crocheron family, among them Joseph Crocheron of Staten Island, both figure in the department's account of it. John Golden Park is filed as Q012B, also in Community Board 11.

All Saints Episcopal Church is at 214-35 40th Avenue, and can be reached at 718-229-5631. The neighborhood's Wikipedia article says the church holds "local examples of reputed works executed by Louis Comfort Tiffany." The Bayside Historical Society, founded in 1964, prints its own address as 208 Totten Avenue, Fort Totten, Bayside, NY 11359, and states that it began "with three goals: The preservation and restoration of the Lawrence Family Cemetery , Alley Pond and Fort Totten."

sections.heading: Getting there
sections.body:
The Long Island Rail Road's Port Washington Branch calls at Bayside.

Crocheron Park lies along the Cross Island Parkway between 33rd and 35th Avenues, in ZIP 11361. All Saints Episcopal Church is at 214-35 40th Avenue and answers on 718-229-5631. The 111th Precinct station house is at 45-06 215th Street.

The four individual landmarks are addressed at 216th Street and 42nd Avenue (the Lawrence Graveyard), 39-24 to 39-26 213th Street (the Ahles House), 215-37 to 215-43 43rd Avenue and 42-22 to 42-38 216th Street (Hawthorne Court Apartments), and 35-34 Bell Boulevard (the cobblestone house). The Bayside Historical Society prints its own address as 208 Totten Avenue, Fort Totten, Bayside, NY 11359.

faq.question: How do I get to Bayside?
faq.answer: By rail: the Long Island Rail Road's Port Washington Branch calls at Bayside, which is in Community District 11 in northeastern Queens. Crocheron Park lies along the Cross Island Parkway between 33rd and 35th Avenues, and the 111th Precinct station house is at 45-06 215th Street.

faq.question: What are Bayside's designated landmarks?
faq.answer: Four individual New York City landmarks stand in Bayside: the Lawrence Graveyard at 216th Street and 42nd Avenue; the John William and Lydia Ann Bell Ahles House at 39-24 to 39-26 213th Street; Hawthorne Court Apartments at 215-37 to 215-43 43rd Avenue and 42-22 to 42-38 216th Street; and the cobblestone house at 35-34 Bell Boulevard, which its designation report places "on a commercial street in Bayside, Queens."

faq.question: Where is the Bayside Historical Society?
faq.answer: The Society prints its address as 208 Totten Avenue, Fort Totten, Bayside, NY 11359. It was founded in 1964, in its own words "with three goals: The preservation and restoration of the Lawrence Family Cemetery , Alley Pond and Fort Totten." Its archive covers the history of Bayside, Queens, and its adjacent communities.

faq.question: Is Alley Pond Park in Bayside?
faq.answer: Alley Pond Park borders Bayside along the neighborhood's eastern edge. On the origin of the "Alley" name, the Landmarks Preservation Commission's report on 35-34 Bell Boulevard records that "Initially, access was from Little Neck Bay, by boat, or via a road called the “Alley” that ran along the shore." The Bayside Historical Society counts Alley Pond among the three preservation goals it was founded on in 1964.

faq.question: What is on Bell Boulevard?
faq.answer: The Bayside Village Business Improvement District's district runs along Bell Boulevard between Northern Boulevard and 35th Avenue, and the BID says it is "served by Community Board #11" and by the 111th Precinct. The cobblestone house at 35-34 Bell Boulevard, a designated New York City landmark, stands on the same street; its designation report places it "on a commercial street in Bayside, Queens."

photos.title: Gazebo at the eastern end of Crocheron Park
photos.description: A brick gazebo with a green shingled roof and white latticework arches, standing on a paved terrace edged by low brick walls and benches. Bare trees surround it, and water is visible through the branches on the right under a cloudy sky.
photos.author: Meelar

places.summary: A designated New York City landmark house, known as the Cobblestone House. Its Landmarks Preservation Commission designation report places it "on a commercial street in Bayside, Queens."

places.name: Hawthorne Court Apartments
places.summary: A designated New York City landmark apartment complex, addressed by the Landmarks Preservation Commission as 215-37 to 215-43 43rd Avenue and 42-22 to 42-38 216th Street. Benjamin Braunstein designed it; its brickwork is laid in monk bond and its roofs are jerkinheads.
places.history: The complex took a Queens Chamber of Commerce award in 1931.

photos.title: Hawthorne Court Apartments
photos.description: Brick and stucco buildings with dark red half-timbering and window trim, under steep slate roofs with gables and dormers. A stone arch under a peaked slate hood frames the entrance, a lantern hangs beside it, and a lawn with clipped hedges and an iron-railed walk runs along the front.
photos.author: DanTD

The same report records that "Very few 19th century houses survive in Bayside."

photos.title: John William and Lydia Ann Bell Ahles House
photos.description: A two-storey house faced in ochre stucco, with tall white-framed windows set under moulded lintels and a mansard roof clad in scalloped shingles with dormers cut into it. Bare trees and overhead wires cross the view, and cars are parked at the kerb.
photos.author: DanTD

places.name: All Saints Episcopal Church
places.summary: An Episcopal parish church at 214-35 40th Avenue, reachable at 718-229-5631. The neighborhood's Wikipedia article says the building holds "local examples of reputed works executed by Louis Comfort Tiffany."

The BID says the district is "served by Community Board #11" and by the 111th Precinct. places.name: Bayside Historical Society
places.summary: The Bayside Historical Society, founded in 1964, whose archive covers the history of Bayside, Queens, and its adjacent communities. The Society prints its own address as 208 Totten Avenue, Fort Totten, Bayside, NY 11359.
places.history: The Society states that it was founded "with three goals: The preservation and restoration of the Lawrence Family Cemetery , Alley Pond and Fort Totten." The Society directs visitors to its own premises by the Q13 and Q16 buses.

places.summary: A house at 221-04 Corbett Road. Barney Nagler wrote about it in The New York Times of September 1, 1985, under the title "Gentleman In The House On Corbett Road."

places.name: Cornell-Appleton House

places.name: 111th Precinct station house
places.summary: The NYPD's 111th Precinct station house, at 45-06 215th Street. The precinct also serves neighboring Douglaston, and the Bayside Village Business Improvement District names it as the district's precinct.

places.name: Benjamin N. Cardozo High School
places.summary: A New York City public high school in Bayside.

places.name: Bayside station
places.summary: The Long Island Rail Road station serving the neighborhood, on the Port Washington Branch.
places.history: The Bell family donated the land for the station. Abraham Bell had acquired land in Bayside in 1824 and worked a farm of 246 acres.

places.name: Alley Pond Park
places.summary: NYC Parks carries Alley Pond Park as a Flagship Park of 635.514 acres, acquired on August 16, 1934, and gives its location as Little Neck Bay to Springfield Blvd, Union Tpke. Its park ID is Q001 and it spans ZIP codes 11361, 11362, 11363, 11364 and 11426.
places.history: The park is not administratively part of any neighborhood: the Department of City Planning gives it its own 2020 tabulation area, QN1191. It borders Bayside, Douglaston-Little Neck and Oakland Gardens-Hollis Hills.
